\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}
\label{ch:ka-asking-age}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone how old they are in Kannada and give my own age in return.}

Ask \kn{ನಿನ್ನ} \kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \kn{ಎಷ್ಟು}? and answer \kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು} — a complete verbless exchange about age.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ನಿನ್ನ} \kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \kn{ಎಷ್ಟು}?]{\kn{ನಿನ್ನ} \kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \kn{ಎಷ್ಟು}? — \textquotedblleft{}your age, how much?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C19-vayassu}



\begin{quote}
Here's a genuinely nice callback: the Sanskrit word behind Kannada's \textquotedblleft{}age\textquotedblright{} is a distant cousin of a Latin word you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು}} (\emph{vayassu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{age}\textquotedblright{}) comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{वयस्}} (\emph{vayas}, \textquotedblleft{}age, youth, vigor, strength\textquotedblright{}), which traces back to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{wéyh\textsubscript{1}os}. That PIE root is the \textbf{same} one behind Latin \textbf{vīs}, \textquotedblleft{}force, strength, vigor\textquotedblright{} — so Sanskrit's word for \textquotedblleft{}age\textquotedblright{} and Latin's word for \textquotedblleft{}force\textquotedblright{} are genuine, distant cousins, both carrying the older sense of \textquotedblleft{}vigor, life-force\textquotedblright{} before splitting toward different specific meanings.}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a simple possessive, no verb}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನಿನ್ನ} \kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \kn{ಎಷ್ಟು}?} — \textquotedblleft{}How old are you?\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your age — how much?}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ninna vayassu eṣṭu?})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು} \kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು}.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my age {[}is{]} twenty}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nanna vayassu ippattu.})
\end{quote}

Just like Arabic's \emph{ʿumr}, this is a \textbf{verbless} construction in the present tense — Kannada simply states \textquotedblleft{}your age\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}how much,\textquotedblright{} with no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} needed. But notice the shape is simpler than Arabic's: no possessive suffix fused onto the noun, just the ordinary possessive word \textbf{\kn{ನಿನ್ನ}} (\emph{ninna}, \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) sitting in front of \textbf{\kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vayassu\textquotedblright{} — age
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ninna vayassu eṣṭu?\textquotedblright{} — how old are you?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna vayassu ippattu\textquotedblright{} — I am twenty, \textquotedblleft{}my age {[}is{]} twenty\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit word is \textbf{\kn{ವಯಸ್ಸು}} from, and what Latin word is its PIE cousin? (\textbf{\dv{वयस्}}, \emph{vayas}, \textquotedblleft{}age/vigor\textquotedblright{} — cousin of Latin \textbf{vīs}, \textquotedblleft{}force,\textquotedblright{} both from PIE \emph{wéyh\textsubscript{1}os.) Does Kannada use a verb to state age? (\textbf{No} — \textquotedblleft{}your age how-much,\textquotedblright{} no verb needed.) How do you say \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty\textquotedblright{}? (}Nanna vayassu ippattu\emph{ — \textquotedblleft{}my age {[}is{]} twenty.\textquotedblright{})}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anusvara]{\kn{◌ಂ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S123-sign-anusvara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಚ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ಂ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ಂ}} — \emph{a nasal, ridden on the syllable before it}.

It is a \textbf{nasal}, written as a mark rather than as a letter. It rides on the syllable before it and turns the end of it nasal.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{◌ಂ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} \emph{santōṣa} — joy / pleased to meet you
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಎರಡು} \kn{ಮೂರು} \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು} \kn{ಐದು}} \emph{ondu eraḍu mūru nālku aidu} — one to five
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಆರು} \kn{ಏಳು} \kn{ಎಂಟು} \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು} \kn{ಹತ್ತು}} — six to ten
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಗಂಟೆ}} \emph{gaṇṭe} — hour — the SAME Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} word behind Hindi's ghantā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ಂ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ಂ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌ಂ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌ಂ} three times, humming the nasal at the end of the syllable as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{◌ಂ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{◌ಂ}? What does it add to the syllable before it? (\textbf{A nasal.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
